Newly hatched nestlings of the Blue-throated bee-eater emerge at a remarkably modest size, with a wet weight at birth of approximately 4.17 grams [Wwb = approximately 4.17 grams], placing them among the lighter offspring of the genus Merops. This initial mass is characteristic of altricial young that depend entirely on intensive biparental provisioning during the early post-hatching phase. The incubation period, during which eggs are held at a constant 36 °C [T = 36 °C], proceeds for approximately 23 days [ab = approximately 23 days] before hatching occurs, a duration that aligns well with findings for the closely related European bee-eater, Merops apiaster, whose incubation typically spans from three to four weeks. Upon emergence, the naked and blind chicks are brooded continuously by the female while the male undertakes frequent foraging trips to deliver small aerial insects, predominantly dragonflies and bees. The relatively low birth mass underscores the energetic constraints operating during early development, as the parents must partition their efforts between thermoregulatory care and prey capture within often thermally demanding environments.

Once the initial brooding phase is complete, the developing altricial nestling enters a period of rapid somatic growth, transitioning gradually from a completely dependent state to one capable of endothermic regulation. Under typical thermal conditions, particularly when ambient temperatures approach 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the fledging milestone is achieved at approximately 30 days following hatching [tx = approximately 30 days following hatching]. This comparatively short nestling period reflects the species' adaptation to tropical and subtropical latitudes where aerial insect prey remains abundant during the breeding season, enabling parents to deliver sufficient calories to sustain the chick's precipitous weight gain. By the time of nest departure, the young bee-eater has increased its body mass substantially from the initial 4.17 grams [Wwb = 4.17 grams] at hatching, though it remains short of the dimensions of a fully mature adult. Fledging is a critical juncture; the young bird must quickly master aerial foraging techniques, often receiving supplemental feedings from its parents for another week or two beyond nest exit.

The transition from fledgling to a sexually maturing subadult involves a prolonged period of anatomical and physiological refinement, particularly in the development of the flight apparatus and the gonadal tissues. Onset of reproductive maturity occurs approximately 90 days after hatching [tp = approximately 90 days after hatching], a value that has been documented under field conditions where ambient temperatures regularly reach 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This relatively rapid attainment of puberty is a common trait among tropical bee-eaters, as the extended breeding seasons and stable food supply reduce the necessity for a protracted juvenile stage. During this subadult phase, immature individuals often join non-breeding flocks, honing their aerial acrobatics and cooperative foraging strategies before attempting to establish a territory or attract a mate. The morphological changes accompanying sexual maturation include the full development of the elongated central tail feathers and the deepening of the vivid blue and green plumage that characterizes the species. By the time the bird approaches its first full year, it is typically indistinguishable in appearance and size from older breeding adults.

First reproduction in the Blue-throated bee-eater is typically deferred until the bird is approximately one calendar year of age, corresponding to a time since birth at first brood of 365 days [tR = 365 days] under conditions where average body temperatures during active metabolic periods remain near 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This timing places the species at the early end of the iteroparous spectrum among coraciiform birds, as many larger kingfishers and rollers take two or more years to begin breeding. The first nesting attempt is often characterized by a smaller clutch size compared to subsequent years, reflecting the inexperience of the younger pair and their lower foraging efficiency during the demanding provisioning period. Reproductive output in these initial broods is modest; females typically produce 1 clutch per year [F_R_i = 1 clutch per year], with an average clutch size of approximately 4 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 4 eggs per clutch]. This annual reproductive rate translates to a moderate lifetime fecundity given the species' longevity, as the costs associated with excavation of nest tunnels in sandy banks and the risks of predation constrain the frequency of nesting events.

Longevity data for Merops viridis, extrapolated from field studies of the congeneric white-fronted bee-eater, Merops bullockoides, suggest that the maximum lifespan in the wild is on the order of 7 years [am = 7 years] when individuals are subject to the typical thermal regime of 40 °C [T = 40 °C] during their active metabolic periods. This lifespan is consistent with that of other medium-sized insectivorous birds inhabiting stable tropical environments, where high adult survival is favored over a strategy of extreme annual fecundity. Over the course of a 7-year (7 years) [am = 7 years] reproductive lifespan, an individual female may successfully fledge multiple broods, as her annual reproductive effort comprises a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year] with 4 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 4 eggs per clutch] at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult, approximately 32.3 grams [Wwi = approximately 32.3 grams], reflects a body plan optimized for the rapid, agile pursuit of flying insects, with a relatively low wing loading that facilitates sustained aerial hawking. This asymptotic mass is attained within the first year of life, well before the bird embarks on its first reproductive season. The species thus exemplifies a life-history strategy centered on moderate, consistent reproductive effort and high adult survival, traits that are finely tuned to the predictable resource availability of tropical lowland forests and open woodlands.
